sections.h2: Choosing how to sell an Orlando house
sections.html:
Orlando sellers can take a cash offer, hire an agent or sell directly. The best fit depends on how much work the house needs and whether a historic district rule covers the address. The city had an estimated 333,888 residents in July 2025, and its homes range from downtown condos to bungalows built in the 1920s.

  • Cash offers suit houses with deferred repairs, tenant trouble or a tight deadline, since no lender stands between you and closing.
  • A traditional listing suits a house that shows well and can handle rounds of open houses.
  • A direct sale suits an owner with a buyer already in mind, perhaps a neighbor or the current tenant.

Before you choose, find out whether your street sits inside one of the city's six historic preservation districts. A district limits what the next owner can do to the exterior, and buyers will ask.

Renters outnumber owners here: only 39.5% of homes are owner-occupied. Investors with rental plans are regular bidders, and plenty of sellers own rentals themselves.

  • Residents, mid-2025: 333,888, up 8.4% since April 2020
  • Households: 131,179
  • Midpoint value of an owned home: $394,100
  • Owner cost per month with a mortgage: $2,231
  • Typical rent per month: $1,747

The city covers more than 110 square miles, so values differ a great deal from one neighborhood to the next. Treat the midpoint as a rough reference and get a price opinion for your own street.

Downtown Orlando grew around Lake Eola. Jacob Summerlin bought 200 acres there in 1873, and the Summerlin family donated land around the shore in 1883. The lake became a public park in 1888.

The land north of the lake was planted in citrus until the freezes of 1894 and 1895 destroyed the groves, and it was then subdivided for homes. Lake Eola Heights grew most between 1905 and 1925. Colonialtown South was platted in part in 1883, and most of its houses went up during the 1920s land boom. Houses from those eras turn up often among sale listings, and their age is why the district rules below matter.

sections.h2: Does a historic district change how I sell?
sections.html:
It can. A house in one of Orlando's six local historic preservation overlay districts needs city approval before exterior changes. The city's Orlando Locator, which takes an address, shows whether you live in a district. Most districts require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Preservation Board. The Downtown Historic District uses a Certificate of Appearance Approval from the Appearance Review Board.

Orlando local historic districts and review time for minor work

Downtown198010 to 15 days

Lake Copeland19842 to 10 days

• Major work such as additions, new construction, relocation and demolition goes to a board hearing. Plan on about seven weeks.
  • Lake Eola Heights does not require approval for landscaping, paint color, or patios and walkways out of public view.
  • In Lake Copeland, approval is not needed for work that needs no city building permit or for structures built after January 1, 1940.
  • Chain-link fencing is restricted in Lake Eola Heights and Lake Lawsona.

On August 10, 2026 the City Council approved a 36-month temporary change that moves reviews of new or renovated downtown projects from the Historic Preservation Board to the Appearance Review Board. Questions go to the Historic Preservation Officer at 407.246.3416 or to Permitting at 407.246.2271. If a buyer plans exterior work, a call to one of those lines before you accept an offer can save a surprise later.

sections.h2: Tax break for rehabilitated historic homes
sections.html: Orlando adopted a property tax exemption in 1994 for the substantial rehabilitation of locally designated historic property. It runs 10 years and covers 100 percent of the city's share of the tax tied to the value added by the rehabilitation. The exemption stays in place when the property sells. If your house has had that work done, mention it in the listing and keep the paperwork for the buyer.

sections.h2: Homestead and your tax bill at sale
sections.html:
Homestead lowers a home's taxable value by as much as $50,000. On the Orange County Property Appraiser's website there is a tax estimator built for people thinking of buying or selling. Tax bills go out every November, and the biggest early-payment discount goes to whoever pays that month.

When you sell, your homestead ends. The new owner files a fresh application by March 1, and the assessor resets the value to just value, as it does after any sale, foreclosure or title transfer (spouses and some transfers at death are exceptions). Moving to another Florida home? Portability lets you carry part of your capped assessment over, provided you set it up within three years.

Some owners hold added breaks that the buyer will not inherit. A local ordinance can give people 65 and older an extra exemption of up to $50,000 within an income limit, and a person with a permanent service-connected disability may receive a discount matching the VA rating. Ask the property appraiser what applies to you.

The state's deed tax is $0.70 per $100 of consideration, and Orange County charges the standard amount. Whoever signs the deed answers for the tax, whatever the sales contract says, and the clerk takes payment when the deed goes on record. Page count, the number of names and technology add-ons drive recording fees, which are billed on top. Your closing statement will show the final figure.

sections.h2: Selling with a tenant in the house
sections.html: If someone rents your house, that sets the pace. Ending a year-to-year tenancy takes 60 days' notice in Florida, and once a court sides with the landlord the sheriff gives 24 hours of posted notice before possession returns. Investors often buy houses with tenants inside, so a lease need not block a sale. Pull together the lease, the rent ledger and deposit records first, since every buyer asks.

A cash sale skips the loan approval and the lender's appraisal, so the usual delays tied to a buyer's financing drop out. You still need clear title, a signed deed and a closing agent to record it. Ask for the closing date in writing, and confirm who pays for the deed stamps and recording before you sign.

For an old house, ask whether the buyer will take it as is. That means no repair requests after inspection, and you should confirm it in the contract, not on a phone call.

faqs.q: How can I tell whether my address is in a historic district?
faqs.a: Enter your address in the Orlando Locator on the city's website, or call the Historic Preservation Officer at 407.246.3416. Six local districts exist: Downtown, Lake Cherokee, Lake Copeland, Lake Eola Heights, Lake Lawsona and Colonialtown South.

faqs.q: How long do historic approvals take?
faqs.a: Minor work can clear a quick review in 2 to 10 days in most districts and 10 to 15 days downtown. Major work needs a board hearing, and the city says to plan on about seven weeks.

faqs.q: Does my Save Our Homes cap pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. A sale is a change of ownership, so the county returns the property to just value. The buyer applies for a fresh homestead by March 1 if they live there on January 1.

faqs.q: What is the stamp tax on a deed in Orange County?
faqs.a: It is $0.70 per $100 of consideration, paid through the clerk at recording. Your closing agent can quote the exact amount.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited Orlando house quickly?
faqs.a: Often, once the estate has authority to sell. Florida offers a simplified summary administration for some smaller or older estates, and creditor claims have their own cutoff dates. A probate attorney can confirm which path your estate takes.
